articles.author: kevindev
articles.description:
Email verification looks like a small feature: create a token, send a message, and accept the link. In a backend service, it is a stateful authentication workflow with retries, expiry, duplicate requests, and untrusted delivery infrastructure. Treating it as only an email-sending problem makes the REST API harder to reason about.
The result are familiar: a link works twice, a delayed message verifies an old account, or a retry creates several valid tokens. A replay ledger gives the service one durable place to answer a simple question: what happened to this verification attempt?
A verification request usually crosses four boundaries:
The client asks the REST API to start verification.
The API records an attempt and queues a message.
A mail provider delivers a link to a mailbox.
The client …
articles.title: A Replay Ledger for REST Email Verification

articles.author: Dave Mille
articles.description:
Keeping DeepTutor's Local Inference Alive Past the Twelfth Turn


The page landed at 3:12 a.m. vLLM in front of DeepTutor had been OOM-killed on turn twelve of a calculus session, and the restart threw away the thread that lesson had just built. The weights were fine. The KV cache was not.
I integrate HKUDS/DeepTutor from the outside. I do not maintain the graph. The point of the stack is a lifelong loop: student state, skill traces, and a planner that still knows what the learner missed last week. The model call is a replaceable backend. The failure is inference quietly exhausting GPU memory because the KV cache was sized for a demo and left up across real lessons.
A 70B at Q4 or AWQ fits two 48 GB cards until you preallocate a 32k cache and let sessions pile up prefixes that never repeat…
articles.title: Keeping DeepTutor's Local Inference Alive Past the Twelfth Turn

articles.description:
Request the same product page from a US server and from a German residential IP, and you will often get two different pages. The price may be in euros, an item may be out of stock, the search results may be reordered, or you may be redirected to /de/. If your scraper runs from a US cloud box, you only ever see the US version, which is no help when you need what a shopper in Berlin or Mumbai sees.
This post covers how sites guess your location, how country- and city-level proxy targeting works, and the Python code (requests, httpx, and Playwright) for getting geo-specific content reliably. The ideas apply to any language.
Prices and currency change most frequently, and some retailers run different promotions in different regions.
Stock and delivery windows will vary, and some pages will sta…

articles.description:
There is a particularly interesting inconvenience in using your own poetry as a machine learning dataset: you know what the words were supposed to mean.
Whether they actually convey that meaning is a different question entirely.
I recently decided to turn twelve of my poems into numerical vectors and investigate what happened to the relationships between them. It began as a fairly innocent exercise in curiosity and ended up making me reconsider how I evaluate semantic retrieval systems.
Somewhere in between, three embedding models and I had a disagreement about a mountain.
In one of my poems, I wrote about a painter who had become disillusioned with painting reality.

light resting temporarily on bone.

articles.author: yutianle
articles.description:
Prioritizing CVE-2026-123633 across internet-facing reverse proxies


Not every NGINX asset deserves the same response, even when it matches the vulnerable version range. A useful priority model for CVE-2026-123633 combines internet reachability, HTTP/2 proxying, connection pressure, and patch evidence.
F5's K000163928 advisory describes a use-after-free in ngx_http_v2_module, categorized as CWE-416. F5 assigns CVSS v3.1 8.1 and CVSS v4.0 9.2. The confirmed impact includes denial of service, while code execution depends on ASLR being disabled or bypassed.
Affected NGINX Open Source releases span 1.19.7 through 1.31.8. The fixed releases are 1.30.7 and 1.31.9. NGINX Plus and bundled products have separate patch rows in the advisory.
F5 says the worker must be low on worker_connections while…
articles.title: Prioritizing CVE-2026-123633 across internet-facing reverse proxies

articles.author: Juan Manuel Garrido
articles.description:
A burst pipe at 3 AM is a useful test case for any AI agent you put in front of customers. The agent can handle almost every step around the problem. It cannot do the one step that matters: someone has to go to the house and fix it.
That makes the handoff the most important piece of the design, and it is usually the least specified.
I run EGA Futura, a native ERP on Salesforce, and co-founded Vantegrate, an AI agent company, with Francisco Morales. In a LinkedIn post I wrote in Spanish today, I noted that AI now writes code, analyzes contracts and builds apps, while a broken pipe in the middle of the night still needs a person who shows up. For engineers, that sentence becomes a requirement: design the agent so the human who shows up gets everything they need, and nothing the agent guessed…

articles.author: testingaga
articles.description:
In the mid-2010s, anonymous social platforms like Whisper and Yik Yak captured tens of millions of users. They promised an unfiltered digital void where people could admit their deepest regrets, mental health battles, and campus secrets without the burden of their real-world identities.
Yet, almost every single one of those platforms collapsed. 
The failure was not due to a lack of demand—humans have an innate psychological need for candid emotional expression. The failure was architectural:
Unmoderated Open-Text Comments: Anonymity without structural guardrails inevitably breeds targeted cyberbullying.
Hyper-Local Geofencing: Restricting posts to a 5-mile radius allowed users to identify dorm rooms and specific individuals.
Database & Metadata Leaks: Legacy platforms stored unencrypted ge…
articles.title: Architecting Zero-Knowledge Anonymity: Building a Safe, Bullying-Free Confession Platform

articles.author: Matthew J. Moore
articles.description:
I've been answering Windows activation questions on Microsoft's Q&A forum lately, mostly because I deal with this stuff all day anyway. Every question there now gets an AI answer automatically. And honestly? They're good. Well written, accurate, links to the right docs.
Today a guy posted that his Windows key stopped working after he swapped in a new hard drive. The AI answer was textbook: install the same edition, sign in with your Microsoft account, run the activation troubleshooter. All correct.
It didn't fix anything.
What actually happened took about ten comments to dig out. The "key" he'd saved before swapping drives was a placeholder, not his real one, so a key checker called it invalid and he thought his license was gone. The troubleshooter showed zero PCs on his account, even thou…
articles.title: The AI's answer was correct. Why did it still take 10 comments to fix his problem?
